stem: What is healthspan?
choices: Years lived after the retirement age
Years a cell divides before dying
explanation: Lifespan is total years; healthspan is years without chronic disease. The goal is morbidity compression: more vital years.

stem: What does 'morbidity compression' aim for?
choices: Squeezing illness into fewer final years
Shortening the time spent in hospital care
explanation: Morbidity compression means pushing chronic disease into a shorter period at the end of life, so more years are lived healthy.

stem: Two 70-year-olds have the same lifespan so far, but one has had diabetes and heart disease since 50. Which measure differs between them?
explanation: Same chronological age and lifespan so far; the one with 20 years of chronic disease has a shorter healthspan.

stem: According to the course, what drove the historical rise in human life expectancy?
choices: Lower birth rates and smaller families
Genetic selection and engineering of the population
explanation: Life expectancy rose dramatically through sanitation, vaccines and healthcare, with antibiotics and nutrition also important.

stem: Roughly how much of the ageing rate does the course estimate is influenced by lifestyle and nutrition?
explanation: Take-home: biological ageing is modifiable; about 70% of the ageing rate is influenced by lifestyle and nutrition, not fixed genetics.

stem: How many hallmarks of ageing are in the 2023 López-Otín 'playbook'?
explanation: The 2023 Cell paper proposes twelve hallmarks (up from nine in 2013). The course's simplified list has six.

stem: Which is one of the 12 hallmarks of ageing?
explanation: The twelve: genomic instability, telomere attrition, epigenetic alterations, loss of proteostasis, disabled macroautophagy, deregulated nutrient sensing, mitochondrial dysfunction, cellular senescence, stem cell exhaustion, altered intercellular communication, chronic inflammation and dysbiosis.

stem: Which hallmark describes chromosome ends shortening with each cell division?
explanation: Telomere attrition: telomeres shorten with each division. Genomic instability is accumulated DNA damage; epigenetic alterations are methylation changes.

stem: Which hallmark is the decline of the cell's 'recycling system', so damaged organelles build up?
explanation: Disabled macroautophagy: the recycling system declines. Loss of proteostasis is failing protein quality control and misfolded proteins.

stem: Senescent cells harm their neighbours by secreting what?
explanation: Cellular senescence: senescent ('zombie') cells secrete SASP, which accelerates ageing in neighbouring cells and drives inflammaging.

stem: Which hallmark involves mTOR hyperactivation with AMPK and sirtuin decline?
explanation: Deregulated nutrient sensing: mTOR hyperactivation, AMPK/sirtuin decline. This is what resveratrol (SIRT1, AMPK) and fasting mimetics target.

stem: Mitochondria that accumulate mutations lead to which pair of changes?
choices: More NAD+ and less DNA damage
explanation: Mitochondrial dysfunction: mutations reduce ATP production and increase reactive oxygen species.

stem: What is 'inflammaging'?
choices: An acute fever in elderly patients
An allergy that first appears after age 60
The ageing of the skin by UV light
explanation: Inflammaging is persistent low-grade inflammation driven by SASP, leading to frailty, chronic disease and cognitive decline.

stem: What is immunosenescence?
choices: Age-related decline of the immune system
A faster immune response in older adults
An immune reaction to a vaccine
explanation: Immunosenescence is the ageing and collapse of immune defence (thymic involution, senescent cells), alongside inflammaging.

stem: Which method does the course call the most accurate predictor of biological age?
choices: Body mass index and waist circumference
explanation: Epigenetic clocks (DNA methylation at CpG sites, e.g. Horvath, GrimAge) are the most accurate. Telomere length and the Levine PhenoAge blood panel (9 tests) are the other methods.

stem: A pharmacy wants a cheap biological-age test from 9 standard blood markers such as hsCRP, HbA1c and albumin. Which method is this?
explanation: The Levine PhenoAge computes biological age from 9 standard blood tests (hsCRP, HbA1c, homocysteine, albumin, IGF-1…).

stem: What are reactive oxygen species (ROS)?
choices: Oxygen molecules that damage cells in excess
explanation: Cells naturally produce ROS; in excess they damage proteins, DNA, lipids and mitochondria, contributing to ageing.

stem: What is the course's position on antioxidants?
choices: More antioxidants always means longer life
Balance, not elimination, is the goal
Oxidation is always harmful to cells
explanation: ROS at low levels are essential signals (Nrf2 defence, immunity, exercise adaptation: hormesis). 'More antioxidants = longer life' is incomplete and exaggerated.

stem: An athlete megadoses antioxidants to 'remove all free radicals'. Why might this backfire?
choices: Free radicals are only made in cancer cells
Low ROS signals drive exercise adaptation
explanation: At low levels ROS trigger Nrf2 defence and exercise adaptation (hormesis). Eliminating them removes a useful signal; food antioxidants beat high-dose isolates.

stem: Which endogenous enzyme converts superoxide to hydrogen peroxide as the first line of mitochondrial defence?
explanation: SOD converts superoxide to H₂O₂; catalase converts H₂O₂ to water; glutathione is the master antioxidant; CoQ10 works in electron transport.

stem: Which endogenous antioxidant converts hydrogen peroxide into water?
explanation: Catalase: H₂O₂ to water, protecting the peroxisome. SOD makes the H₂O₂ in the first place; Nrf2 is the master regulator of 200+ antioxidant genes.

stem: Which molecule does the course call the 'master cellular antioxidant' that regenerates vitamins C and E?
explanation: Glutathione is the master antioxidant; it regenerates vitamins C and E and supports phase II detox.

stem: Which is described as the most potent endogenous antioxidant, declining with age?
explanation: Melatonin: the most potent endogenous antioxidant, protects mitochondria, declines with age. Vitamin C is dietary, not endogenous.

stem: A patient on statins asks which antioxidant the drug depletes. The answer is…
explanation: CoQ10 works in mitochondrial electron transport, regenerates vitamin E, and is depleted by statins.

stem: Why is plain oral glutathione a weak supplement?
choices: It is degraded in the gut before absorption
It is toxic to the liver at any dose
It is stored permanently in body fat
It only works when it is injected into muscle
explanation: Oral glutathione has low bioavailability because it is broken down in digestion. Liposomal forms (about 90% vs 10–15%) or IV drips are the workarounds.

stem: What recent concern about glutathione does the course raise?
choices: It causes scurvy in the elderly
explanation: Research suggests glutathione could be a double-edged sword, potentially feeding and protecting cancer cells in active cancers.

stem: Class notes warn that giving iron to an anaemic patient with a bacterial infection can backfire because…
choices: The bacteria use the iron to grow
Iron blocks the absorption of antibiotics
explanation: Iron supplements during infection can feed the bacteria, which compete for iron and grow more aggressive.

stem: Which Thai superfood is rich in anthocyanins?
explanation: Butterfly pea: anthocyanins. Holy basil: rosmarinic acid, eugenol. Galangal: galangin flavonoids. Mangosteen: xanthones.

stem: Which antioxidant is found in mangosteen, with emerging anti-cancer evidence?
explanation: Mangosteen contains xanthones. Anthocyanins are butterfly pea; galangin is galangal; eugenol is holy basil.

stem: Which carotenoid is claimed to be 500–6,000× more potent than vitamin E and to cross the blood–brain barrier?
explanation: Astaxanthin: 500–6,000× vitamin E (formulation-dependent), crosses the BBB, reduces mitochondrial ROS (4–12 mg/day).

stem: Which supplement is described as the most potent natural autophagy inducer, mimicking fasting?
explanation: Spermidine: the most potent natural autophagy inducer, mimics fasting, linked to longer lifespan and lower CV mortality.

stem: Which supplement acts as a senolytic, selectively clearing senescent cells?
explanation: Quercetin (senolytic) selectively eliminates senescent cells and reduces SASP; the senolytic protocol pairs quercetin with fisetin, cyclically.

stem: Resveratrol is mainly linked to activating which pathway?
explanation: Resveratrol activates SIRT1/SIRT5 and promotes AMPK (150–500 mg trans-resveratrol a day).

stem: Why are NMN and NR sold instead of NAD+ itself?
choices: NAD+ is illegal to sell in Asia
NAD+ is toxic to the liver
NAD+ is banned as a food ingredient
explanation: Direct oral NAD+ has 2–10% bioavailability (digested before reaching cells), so the market sells precursors (NMN, NR) or IV NAD+.

stem: What did RCTs show for 250 mg/day of NMN?
choices: Telomeres doubled in length in a year
No change in any blood marker
explanation: 250 mg/day NMN raised blood NAD+ by about 38% and improved muscle endurance. NMN is mainstream in Japan (sold in convenience stores).

stem: Which country has the most advanced NMN/NAD+ market, with NMN sold in convenience stores?
explanation: Japan: NMN mass market, 150+ companies. Thailand: the world's largest per-capita drinkable collagen market. Singapore: biotech longevity. Korea: K-longevity and red ginseng.

stem: Thailand leads the world per capita in which longevity-beauty product?
explanation: Thailand's collagen economy: world's largest per-capita drinkable collagen market, over USD 180M (2023).

stem: Ashwagandha, ginseng, reishi and rhodiola belong to which supplement category?
explanation: Adaptogens are associated with resilience, stress reduction and overall wellness.

stem: Why does the course link omega-3 to brain ageing?
choices: It supports neuronal and myelin fats
explanation: Omega-3 supports cardiovascular and brain health and lowers inflammation; the myelin sheath is made of fat layers, and class notes say it helps keep fat in ageing neurons.

stem: Alzheimer's disease is characterised by…
choices: Loss of dopamine neurons in the gut
Low vitamin K and bleeding in the brain
explanation: Alzheimer's: amyloid-beta plaques and tau tangles leading to neuroinflammation; changes start 15–20 years before symptoms. Parkinson's: dopaminergic loss and alpha-synuclein.

stem: Which disease involves loss of dopaminergic neurons, with a 'gut-first hypothesis' for where misfolding begins?
explanation: Parkinson's: dopamine neurons degenerate (nigro-striatal pathway), alpha-synuclein aggregates, and the misfolding may begin in the enteric nervous system.

stem: How long before symptoms do Alzheimer's pathological changes begin?
explanation: Pathology begins 15–20 years before symptoms appear, which is the case for early prevention.

stem: Age-related loss of muscle is called…
explanation: Ageing raises the risk of CVD, diabetes and osteoporosis, and contributes to sarcopenia (muscle ageing), dementia and cancer. Class notes: protein and exercise for muscle, vitamin D for bone.

stem: An elderly client asks which nutrients target their bones specifically. Which pair fits?
explanation: Nutrients for healthy ageing: calcium + vitamin D (bones), B12 (energy, brain), protein (muscle), potassium (blood pressure), omega-3 (inflammation), magnesium, zinc (immunity).

stem: By roughly when is Thailand projected to become a 'super-aged' society?
explanation: The course puts super-aged status at 2045 (class notes heard 2035); fertility is falling (under 1.1) and elderly will exceed 12M by 2033.

stem: Where is Thailand's ageing crisis concentrated, and why?
choices: Bangkok, as the elderly move in
The southern islands, due to tourism
Rural areas, as the young migrate
explanation: Rural ageing: young people migrate to cities, leaving elderly care and access to longevity products as a national innovation challenge.

stem: Which is NOT one of the pressures Thailand's ageing creates?
explanation: Ageing plus low fertility means healthcare burden, pension pressure, workforce shortages (under 2 workers per elderly person by 2050) and caregiver shortages.

stem: What do the Blue Zones share?
choices: High-protein diets and structured gym routines
explanation: Blue Zones: about 95% of calories from plants, natural daily movement (walking, gardening), purpose and strong social ties (Okinawa's 'moai'), and stress management.

stem: Which Blue Zone is known for the 'moai', a lifelong social support network?
explanation: Okinawans develop a moai from childhood; Ikarians eat lots of olive oil; Sardinians stay active herding; Nicoya prioritises rest and family.

stem: Which dietary pattern does the course link to lower inflammation, cardiovascular protection and cognitive health?
explanation: The Mediterranean style (vegetables, olive oil, legumes, fish, nuts, moderate calories) contrasts with the American diet of processed food, red meat and sugary drinks.

stem: Which lifestyle factor does the course credit with the largest biological-age reduction?
explanation: Lifestyle stacking: diet 5–12 years, exercise 3–10, stress and social 3–8, sleep 3–7, environment 2–5, supplements only 1–6.

stem: A client wants to 'stop ageing' with supplements alone. What is the course's evidence-based answer?
choices: Only prescription drugs can slow ageing
Ageing is fixed by genetics alone
explanation: Marketing hype vs reality: most supplements may support health but do not 'stop ageing'. The strongest evidence is exercise, sleep, diet, no smoking, stress reduction and social connection.

stem: Which campaign used a digital healthy-ageing assessment tool 2.1 million times and lifted sales 67%?
explanation: Blackmores Thailand (2023): the assessment tool was used 2.1M times, +67% sales. Amway grew CoQ10 and omega-3; Bumrungrad served 4,000+ patients through medical tourism.

stem: The course states that 'more antioxidants = longer life' is scientifically incomplete and exaggerated.
explanation: Oxidation is not always bad; some oxidative signalling is essential. Balance, not elimination.

stem: Parkinson's disease is characterised mainly by amyloid-beta plaques and tau tangles.
explanation: That is Alzheimer's. Parkinson's is loss of dopaminergic neurons and alpha-synuclein aggregation.

stem: Forest bathing (shinrin-yoku) is linked to lower blood pressure and cortisol.
explanation: The Japanese practice decreases blood pressure and cortisol and promotes relaxation, attention and mood.
